goal: Prepare a mid-level software engineer to pass algorithm, system design, and behavioral interviews at Google, Anthropic, and Chewy by January 2027.

resources.CTCI: Cracking the Coding Interview, Gayle Laakmann McDowell — foundational data structures and algorithm patterns with worked examples; ideal warm-up for someone refreshing fundamentals across all topics.
resources.EPI: Elements of Programming Interviews, Aziz/Lee/Prakash — deeper, harder problems organized by topic; use to push from medium to hard difficulty in later phases.
resources.DDIA: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann — core distributed systems concepts (replication, partitioning, consistency) essential for Google and Chewy backend-style system design.
resources.SDI: System Design Interview Vol 1 & 2, Alex Xu — interview-focused walkthroughs of common design problems with clear frameworks; the backbone of system design prep.
resources.GROK: Grokking the Coding Interview patterns — reorganizes LeetCode problems into reusable patterns (sliding window, two pointers, BFS/DFS, etc.) to build transferable intuition.
resources.STAR: Self-authored STAR story bank — a living document of behavioral stories tailored to Google's Googleyness/leadership signals, Anthropic's mission and safety-minded culture, and Chewy's customer-obsession values.

problem_set: Work LeetCode by topic following the fixed topic order, hitting a weekly target and revisiting missed problems with spaced repetition rather than chasing volume.

phases.name: Foundation
phases.focus: Rebuild core fundamentals across arrays, strings, hashing, linked lists, stacks, queues, and basic recursion. Since the candidate wants to work on 'everything,' this phase establishes broad coverage and comfort with reading problems, choosing data structures, and writing clean code under light time pressure. August (largely in this window) is intentionally lighter due to travel.
phases.books: CTCI chapters on data structures and Big-O; GROK patterns for two pointers, sliding window, and fast/slow pointers.
phases.behavioral_focus: Draft 3 initial STAR stories and outline raw material from current Partners Capital projects.

phases.name: Build
phases.focus: Move into trees, graphs, heaps, and intervals while increasing problem difficulty toward consistent medium solves. Introduce structured system design study using a repeatable framework, and begin connecting collaborative system work from the day job into articulable design reasoning.
phases.books: GROK BFS/DFS and tree patterns; EPI tree and graph chapters; begin SDI Vol 1 fundamentals and DDIA chapters on storage and replication.
phases.behavioral_focus: Expand to 6 polished stories and practice the STAR structure aloud, focusing on quantified impact.

phases.name: Depth
phases.focus: Tackle the hardest topics—dynamic programming, backtracking, advanced graphs, and tries—and push into hard problems. Deepen system design with end-to-end designs and tradeoff analysis, leaning on DDIA for distributed systems depth needed at Google and Chewy.
phases.books: EPI dynamic programming and recursion chapters; SDI Vol 2 case studies; DDIA chapters on partitioning, consistency, and consensus.
phases.behavioral_focus: Complete all 8 stories and rehearse follow-up probing questions for each.

phases.name: Polish
phases.focus: Simulate the real interview loop. Do timed mixed-topic problem sets, full mock system design sessions, and behavioral mocks. Identify and close remaining weak spots, and tune communication and time management for Google, Anthropic, and Chewy loops.
phases.books: Re-solve previously missed problems; SDI as quick-reference; review DDIA summaries.
phases.behavioral_focus: Run full behavioral mock interviews and refine delivery, conciseness, and company-value alignment.

behavioral_story_themes: A time you solved an ambiguous, undefined problem from scratch (Google: dealing with ambiguity)
A technical decision where you weighed long-term tradeoffs and reasoned carefully about risk (Anthropic: thoughtful, safety-minded judgment)
A time you went above and beyond to improve the end-user or customer experience (Chewy: customer obsession)
A conflict or disagreement with a senior engineer and how you reached resolution (collaboration and humility)
A project where you took ownership and drove it to completion despite obstacles
A time you made a mistake or shipped a bug, and what you learned and changed
A moment you mentored, taught, or unblocked a teammate (Googleyness: lifting others)
A time you learned a complex new domain or technology quickly under pressure
